question.explanation:
According to the definition of the biconditional,

  • $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ is true if $P \Rightarrow Q$ and $Q \Rightarrow P.$ Otherwise, it is false.

  • In other words, $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ is true if $P$ and $Q$ have the same truth values. Otherwise, it is false.

So, when $A = \textrm F$ and $B = \textrm T,$ we have \begin{align*} (A \Leftrightarrow \neg B) &= (\textrm F \Leftrightarrow \neg \textrm T) \\[3pt] &= (\textrm F \Leftrightarrow \textrm F) \\[3pt] &= \textrm T. \end{align*}

question.text:
\[ P \Leftrightarrow (P \land Q) \equiv \big[P \Rightarrow (P \land Q)\big] \land \bbox[3pt, white, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAAAAAA}} \]

What expression should be inserted into the blank space above to give logically equivalent statements?
question.explanation:
According to the definition of the biconditional,

  • $A \Leftrightarrow B$ is true if $A\Rightarrow B$ and $B\Rightarrow A.$ Otherwise, it is false.

  • In other words, $A \Leftrightarrow B$ is true if $A$ and $B$ have the same truth values. Otherwise, it is false.

So, in this case, we have

\[ P \Leftrightarrow (P \land Q) \equiv \big[P \Rightarrow (P \land Q)\big] \land \big[\,\bbox[2pt, Gainsboro]{\color{blue}(P \land Q) \Rightarrow P}\big]. \]

Therefore, the missing part is $ (P \land Q) \Rightarrow P.$

\[ (P \lor Q) \Leftrightarrow Q \, \equiv \, \bbox[3pt, white, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAAAAAA}} \land \big[Q \Rightarrow (P\lor Q)\big] \]

What expression should be inserted into the blank space above to give logically equivalent statements?
question.explanation:
According to the definition of the biconditional,

  • $A \Leftrightarrow B$ is true if $A\Rightarrow B$ and $B\Rightarrow A.$ Otherwise, it is false.

  • In other words, $A \Leftrightarrow B$ is true if $A$ and $B$ have the same truth values. Otherwise, it is false.

So in this case, we have \[ (P\lor Q) \Leftrightarrow Q \equiv \big[\,\bbox[2pt, Gainsboro]{\color{blue}(P\lor Q) \Rightarrow Q}\big] \land \big[Q \Rightarrow (P\lor Q)\big]. \]

Therefore, the missing part is $(P\lor Q) \Rightarrow Q.$

question.text: $\lnot (R \Leftrightarrow S)\equiv$
question.explanation:
First, we use the definition of the biconditional statement to write the equivalence as a conjunction of implications: \[ \lnot (R \Leftrightarrow S) \equiv \lnot \big((R \Rightarrow S) \land (S \Rightarrow R)\big) \]

Now, we represent all the implications using disjunctions and negations: \[ \lnot \big((R \Rightarrow S) \land (S \Rightarrow R)\big) \equiv \lnot \big((\lnot R \lor S) \land (\lnot S \lor R)\big) \]

Next, we use De Morgan's laws: \begin{align*} \lnot \big( (\lnot R \lor S) \land (\lnot S \lor R)\big) &\equiv \lnot (\lnot R \lor S) \lor \lnot (\lnot S \lor R) \\[3pt] &\equiv (\lnot\lnot R \land \lnot S) \lor (\lnot\lnot S \land \lnot R) \end{align*}

Finally, we simplify the double negations: \begin{align*} (\lnot\lnot R \land \lnot S) \lor (\lnot\lnot S \land \lnot R) &\equiv (R \land \lnot S) \lor (S \land \lnot R) \end{align*}

question.text: $\lnot (A \Leftrightarrow \neg B) \equiv $
question.explanation:
First, we use the definition of the biconditional statement to write the equivalence as a conjunction of implications:

\[ \lnot (A \Leftrightarrow \lnot B) \equiv \lnot \big[(A \Rightarrow \lnot B) \land (\lnot B \Rightarrow A)\big] \]

Now, we represent all the implications using disjunctions and negations:

\[ \lnot \big[(A \Rightarrow \lnot B) \land (\lnot B \Rightarrow A)\big] \equiv \lnot \big[(\lnot A \lor \lnot B) \land (\lnot\lnot B \lor A)\big] \]

Next, we use De Morgan's laws:

\begin{align*} \lnot \big[(\neg A \lor \neg B) \land (\lnot\lnot B \lor A)\big] &\equiv \lnot (\neg A \lor \lnot B) \lor \lnot (\lnot\lnot B \lor A) \\[3pt] &\equiv (\lnot\lnot A \land \lnot\lnot B) \lor (\lnot\lnot\lnot B \land \lnot A) \end{align*}

Finally, we simplify the double negations:

\[ (\lnot\lnot A \land \lnot\lnot B) \lor (\lnot\lnot\lnot B \land \lnot A) \equiv (A \land B) \lor (\lnot B \land \lnot A) \]

question.text: $\lnot (R \Leftrightarrow \neg S)\equiv$
question.explanation:
First, we use the definition of the biconditional statement to write the equivalence as a conjunction of implications: \[ \lnot (R \Leftrightarrow \lnot S) \equiv \lnot \big[(R \Rightarrow \lnot S) \land (\lnot S \Rightarrow R)\big] \]

Now, we represent all the implications using disjunctions and negations: \[ \lnot \big[(R \Rightarrow \lnot S) \land (\lnot S \Rightarrow R)\big] \equiv \lnot \big[(\lnot R \lor \lnot S) \land (\lnot\lnot S \lor R)\big] \]

Next, we simplify the double negations: \[ \lnot \big[(\lnot R \lor \lnot S) \land (\lnot\lnot S \lor R)\big] \equiv \lnot \big[(\lnot R \lor \lnot S) \land (S \lor R)\big] \]

Now, we use De Morgan's laws: \begin{align*} \lnot \big[(\neg R \lor \neg S) \land (S \lor R)\big] &\equiv \lnot (\neg R \lor \lnot S) \lor \lnot (S \lor R) \\[5pt] &\equiv (\lnot\lnot R \land \lnot\lnot S) \lor\lnot (S \lor R) \end{align*}

Finally, we again simplify the double negations and write down symbols in alphabetic order inside the parentheses using commutative laws: \begin{align*} (\lnot\lnot R \land \lnot\lnot S) \lor \lnot (S \lor R) &\equiv (R \land S) \lor \lnot (S \lor R) \\[5pt] &\equiv (R \land S) \lor \lnot (R \lor S) \end{align*}

question.text: $\lnot (P \Leftrightarrow Q) \equiv$
question.explanation:
First, we use the definition of the biconditional statement to write the equivalence as a conjunction of implications:

\[ \lnot (P \Leftrightarrow Q) \equiv \lnot ((P \Rightarrow Q) \land (Q \Rightarrow P)) \]

Now, we represent all the implications using disjunctions and negations:

\[ \lnot ((P \Rightarrow Q) \land (Q \Rightarrow P)) \equiv \lnot ((\lnot P \lor Q) \land (\lnot Q \lor P)) \]

Next, we use De Morgan's laws:

\begin{align*} \lnot ((\lnot P \lor Q) \land (\lnot Q \lor P)) &\equiv \lnot (\lnot P \lor Q) \lor \lnot (\lnot Q \lor P) \\[3pt] &\equiv (\lnot\lnot P \land \lnot Q) \lor (\lnot\lnot Q \land \lnot P) \end{align*}

Finally, we simplify the double negations and write down symbols in alphabetic order inside the parentheses using commutative laws:

\begin{align*} (\lnot\lnot P \land \lnot Q) \lor (\lnot\lnot Q \land \lnot P) \equiv (P \land \lnot Q) \lor (Q \land \lnot P) \\[3pt] \equiv (P \land \lnot Q) \lor (\lnot P \land Q) \\[3pt] \end{align*}

question.text: $\lnot (\lnot X \Leftrightarrow \lnot Y) \equiv $
question.explanation:
First, we use the definition of the biconditional statement to write the equivalence as a conjunction of implications:

\[ \lnot (\lnot X \Leftrightarrow \lnot Y) \equiv \lnot \big[(\lnot X \Rightarrow \lnot Y) \land (\lnot Y \Rightarrow \lnot X)\big] \]

Now, we represent all the implications using disjunctions and negations:

\[ \lnot \big[(\lnot X \Rightarrow \lnot Y) \land (\lnot Y \Rightarrow \lnot X)\big] \equiv \lnot \big[( \lnot \lnot X \lor \lnot Y) \land (\lnot \lnot Y \lor \lnot X)\big] \]

Next, we simplify the double negations: \[ \lnot \big[( \lnot \lnot X \lor \lnot Y) \land (\lnot \lnot Y \lor \lnot X)\big] \equiv \lnot \big[( X \lor \lnot Y) \land (Y \lor \lnot X)\big] \]

Next, we use De Morgan's laws:

\begin{align*} \lnot \big[( X \lor \lnot Y) \land (Y \lor \lnot X)\big] &\equiv \lnot ( X \lor \lnot Y) \lor \lnot (Y \lor \lnot X)\\[3pt] &\equiv ( \lnot X \land \lnot\lnot Y) \lor (\lnot Y \land \lnot\lnot X) \end{align*}

Finally, we again simplify the double negations:

\[ ( \lnot X \land \lnot\lnot Y) \lor (\lnot Y \land \lnot\lnot X) \equiv (\lnot X \land Y) \lor (\lnot Y \land X) \]
